title: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish preacher from Galilee who teaches about the coming kingdom of God, is arrested in Jerusalem and executed by crucifixion on the orders of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. His followers soon proclaim that he has risen from the dead. Most historians accept that he existed and was crucified, but the exact year is uncertain, with AD 30 and 33 the most often proposed.
significance: His followers' belief in his resurrection became the center of Christianity, which spread across the Roman world and is today the world's largest religion.

title: Kushan Empire rises

location.name: Bactria (Kushan homeland; representative point near Balkh)

summary: Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushans, one of the tribes of the Yuezhi people who had moved into Bactria (in today's northern Afghanistan), unites them and begins conquering lands south of the Hindu Kush. His dates are uncertain, and the empire reaches its greatest extent later, under kings such as Kanishka, when it stretches from Central Asia into northern India.
significance: Sitting astride the Silk Road between Rome, Parthia and Han China, the Kushans helped Buddhism and Gandhara art, which blended Greek and Indian styles, spread toward Central Asia and China.

title: Roman conquest of Britain
summary: Emperor Claudius sends an army of some 40,000 men across the Channel, probably landing at Richborough in Kent, and takes the British tribal center of Camulodunum (Colchester). Conquest of the rest of the island is slow and contested, including the revolt of Queen Boudica around AD 60, and Rome never permanently holds the far north of Scotland.
significance: Britain remained a Roman province for nearly four centuries, gaining towns such as London, roads and Hadrian's Wall before Roman rule ended in the early 400s.

title: Buddhism reaches China
summary: According to tradition, Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreams of a golden figure, sends envoys west, and in AD 68 founds the White Horse Temple at Luoyang for two Indian monks who arrive with Buddhist scriptures. The story is legendary in its details; Buddhism probably reached China gradually with merchants and missionaries along the Silk Road, and a Han prince is already recorded supporting Buddhist monks a few years earlier.
significance: Buddhism became one of China's major religions, and from China it spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

title: Destruction of the Second Temple
summary: During a great Jewish revolt against Roman rule, a Roman army under Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, besieges Jerusalem for months, then storms the city and burns the Temple. Much of the city is destroyed, and many of its people are killed or enslaved.
significance: Without the Temple and its sacrifices, Judaism re-centered on synagogues, prayer and the study of scripture led by rabbis, while the Arch of Titus in Rome still shows the Temple's treasures carried off in triumph.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
summary: Mount Vesuvius, near the Bay of Naples, erupts violently and buries the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash, pumice and searing flows of hot gas and rock. Thousands die. The traditional date is 24 August, but some evidence suggests the eruption came a few weeks later, in October.
significance: Rediscovered from the 1700s, the buried towns preserve houses, paintings, shops and graffiti that give an unusually detailed picture of everyday Roman life.

title: Kingdom of Aksum rises
summary: In the highlands of what are now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, the city of Aksum becomes the capital of a growing kingdom. Through its Red Sea port of Adulis it trades ivory, gold and other goods with Rome, Arabia and India, and its rulers later mint their own coins and raise tall carved stone obelisks (stelae).
significance: Aksum became one of the major powers of its age, controlling Red Sea trade, and its culture and Ge'ez script shaped Ethiopia for centuries afterward.

title: Kingdom of Funan
summary: In the lower Mekong region of what is now southern Vietnam and Cambodia, the kingdom known by its Chinese name, Funan, grows rich on sea trade between India and China. At its port of Oc Eo, archaeologists have found Roman coins, Indian beads and Chinese goods. Much of what is known about Funan comes from Chinese records, and its beginnings are uncertain.
significance: Funan is often seen as one of the earliest states of Southeast Asia, and it helped bring Indian ideas about kingship, religion and writing into the region.

title: Moche culture

location.name: Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, near Trujillo

summary: In the river valleys of Peru's dry northern coast, the Moche build irrigation canals, huge adobe-brick pyramids such as the Huaca del Sol, and richly furnished tombs. Their potters make lifelike portrait vessels and pots showing warriors, rituals and daily life.
significance: Moche pottery and metalwork, including the gold of the Lords of Sipan, are among the finest art of the ancient Americas and a key source on Andean life before the Inca.

title: Nazca Lines
summary: On the desert plain of southern Peru, the Nazca people scrape away dark surface stones to make huge figures of animals such as a monkey, a hummingbird and a spider, along with long straight lines and geometric shapes, some best seen from the air. They were made over several centuries, roughly 500 BC to AD 500, and their purpose, perhaps ritual walking paths or links to water and the sky, is still debated.
significance: The lines are among the largest artworks ever made, and their preservation in the dry desert has made them one of the best-known archaeological sites in the Americas.

title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
summary: Cai Lun, an official at the Han court in Luoyang, presents the emperor with paper made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets. Simpler kinds of paper already existed in China, but his method made a cheaper, better writing material, and Chinese tradition credits him as the inventor of paper.
significance: Paper gradually replaced bamboo strips and silk in China, then spread to Korea, Japan, the Islamic world and Europe, eventually making printing and mass literacy possible.

title: Roman Empire at its greatest extent
summary: When Emperor Trajan dies in 117, his conquests of Dacia (in today's Romania) and, briefly, Armenia and Mesopotamia have stretched Roman rule from Britain to the Persian Gulf. His successor Hadrian soon gives up the eastern conquests and turns to defending the borders.
significance: This marked the peak of Roman territorial expansion; afterward the empire mostly defended what it held, a shift symbolized by Hadrian's Wall in Britain.

title: Ptolemy's Almagest
summary: Claudius Ptolemy, a Greek scholar working in Roman Egypt, writes a great treatise on astronomy, later known by its Arabic name, the Almagest. It describes an Earth-centered universe in which the Sun, Moon and planets move on combinations of circles, with tables for predicting their positions.
significance: Translated into Arabic and later Latin, it remained the standard work of astronomy in the Islamic world and Europe for some 1,400 years, until Copernicus and Kepler replaced its Earth-centered model.

title: Yellow Turban Rebellion
summary: Zhang Jue, leader of a Taoist-inspired healing movement, launches a vast peasant uprising across northern and eastern China, his followers wearing yellow headscarves. The Han government crushes the main revolt within a year, but only by relying on regional generals and their private armies.
significance: Those generals became warlords who fought over the weakened Han court, a struggle that ended the dynasty in 220 and led to the Three Kingdoms.

title: Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan
summary: In the Valley of Mexico, the people of Teotihuacan complete the Pyramid of the Sun, one of the largest structures in the ancient Americas, along the city's great central avenue, later called the Avenue of the Dead. The city may already be home to around 100,000 people. Its builders' language and name for the city are unknown; 'Teotihuacan' is the name later given by the Aztecs.
significance: Teotihuacan was one of the largest cities in the world at its height, and its trade, art and influence reached as far as the Maya region.

title: Han dynasty falls; Three Kingdoms

location.name: Xuchang (where the last Han emperor abdicated)

summary: Cao Pi, son of the warlord Cao Cao, forces the last Han emperor to abdicate and declares his own Wei dynasty. Rivals soon proclaim the states of Shu in the southwest and Wu in the southeast, dividing China into three kingdoms that fight for the next six decades.
significance: The end of the Han began some 360 years of division, broken only briefly by the Jin dynasty, and the era's heroes became legends through the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

title: Sasanian Empire founded
summary: Ardashir, a local ruler in Persis (southwestern Iran), defeats and kills the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, and founds the Sasanian dynasty. The new Persian empire, ruled from Ctesiphon in Mesopotamia, is closely tied to the Zoroastrian priesthood.
significance: For four centuries the Sasanians rivaled Rome and Byzantium as a great power, and their art, court culture and government strongly influenced the Islamic caliphates that followed.

title: Classic Maya period begins
summary: In the rainforests of what are now southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, Maya city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan flourish under divine kings. They build stone temples and palaces, and record royal history on carved monuments in a hieroglyphic script, using an advanced calendar and a counting system that includes zero.
significance: The Classic Maya created the most fully developed writing system known from the ancient Americas, along with remarkable achievements in astronomy, mathematics and art.

title: Kofun period in Japan

location.name: Hashihaka Kofun, Nara (one of the earliest great mounds)

summary: In Japan, rulers begin to be buried in huge keyhole-shaped earth mounds, called kofun, surrounded by moats and clay figures (haniwa). The biggest are found around Nara and Osaka, where the Yamato kingdom takes shape as a confederation of powerful clans.
significance: The Yamato rulers of this period are traditionally seen as the ancestors of Japan's imperial line, and their contacts with Korea brought new technologies, and later writing and Buddhism, to Japan.

title: Ghana Empire rises
summary: In the Sahel, in what is now southeastern Mauritania and western Mali, Soninke-speaking people build a kingdom later known as Ghana, after a title of its king. Its origins are poorly documented and may lie earlier or later. It grows rich by taxing trade in gold from the south and salt from the Sahara, carried across the desert by camel caravans.
significance: Ghana was the first of the great West African trading empires, followed by Mali and Songhai; modern Ghana took its name from it, although it lies far to the south.

title: Edict of Milan
summary: Meeting in Milan, the Roman emperors Constantine and Licinius agree to give all people, including Christians, the freedom to worship as they choose, and to return property taken from Christians. It follows the last and harshest persecution of Christians, which an edict of 311 had already ended in part; historians debate whether a formal 'edict' was ever issued in Milan.
significance: With Constantine's backing, Christianity grew from a persecuted minority into the favored religion of the empire, and by 380 its official religion.

title: Gupta Empire founded
summary: Chandragupta I, a king in the Ganges valley, takes the title 'great king of kings' and begins the Gupta era. His successors Samudragupta and Chandragupta II expand the empire across much of northern India.
significance: The Gupta age is often called a classical or golden age of India, with advances in mathematics and astronomy, Sanskrit literature such as Kalidasa's plays, and Hindu and Buddhist art.

title: Council of Nicaea
summary: Emperor Constantine calls Christian bishops from across the empire to Nicaea, in northwestern Anatolia, to settle a bitter dispute over the teachings of Arius, a priest of Alexandria who says Christ the Son was created by God the Father. The council rejects Arius's view and issues a statement of belief, the original Nicene Creed.
significance: It was the first council claiming to speak for the whole church, and the Nicene Creed, in a version expanded in 381, is still recited by most Christian churches.

title: Aksum adopts Christianity
summary: King Ezana of Aksum converts to Christianity, influenced by Frumentius, a Syrian Christian who had been brought to the royal court as a captive and later became the kingdom's first bishop. Aksum's coins begin to show the cross instead of pagan symbols. The exact date of the conversion is uncertain.
significance: Aksum was among the earliest states to adopt Christianity officially, and the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches trace their origins to this conversion.

title: Constantinople founded
summary: Emperor Constantine dedicates the old Greek city of Byzantium, rebuilt and greatly enlarged, as a new imperial capital named Constantinople. It controls the strait of the Bosporus between Europe and Asia and between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
significance: Constantinople was the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for over a thousand years, then of the Ottoman Empire, and as Istanbul remains one of the world's great cities.

title: Huns move west; Migration Period begins
summary: The Huns, nomadic horse archers whose origins are uncertain, move west across the steppe north of the Caspian Sea, defeating the Alans and then the Goths living north of the Black Sea. In 376 large numbers of Goths flee to the Roman frontier on the Danube and are allowed to cross into the empire.
significance: The Huns' advance set off a chain of movements by Germanic and other peoples into the Roman Empire, the so-called Migration Period, which helped bring down the Western Empire and reshape Europe's map.

title: Visigoths sack Rome
summary: The Visigoths, led by their king Alaric, enter Rome and plunder it for three days after the Western Roman government, based at Ravenna, refuses their demands. It is the first time in about 800 years that the city has fallen to a foreign enemy.
significance: The sack shocked the Roman world and prompted Augustine of Hippo to write The City of God, a defense of Christianity that shaped Western thought for centuries.

title: Nalanda university founded
summary: A great Buddhist monastery and center of learning is founded at Nalanda in eastern India, traditionally under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I. It grows into a large residential community of monks and students who study Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine. Calling it a 'university' is a modern comparison, and its founding date is approximate.
significance: Nalanda drew scholars from as far as China, Korea and Central Asia, including the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, and remained a major center of Buddhist learning until its decline around 1200.

title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, and rules Italy as king without naming a new emperor. By then the Western Empire had already lost most of its provinces to Germanic kingdoms.
significance: The date is the traditional end of the ancient world in Western Europe, while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire carries on for nearly another thousand years.

title: Aryabhata's astronomy and mathematics
summary: The Indian astronomer Aryabhata, aged 23 by his own account, completes the Aryabhatiya, a short work in verse on mathematics and astronomy. It works with a place-value number system and gives a value of pi of about 3.1416, early sine tables, and the idea that the Earth spins on its axis.
significance: His work shaped Indian astronomy for centuries and, through Arabic translations, influenced mathematics and astronomy in the Islamic world.

title: Code of Justinian
summary: Emperor Justinian I issues the first version of a new code that gathers and simplifies centuries of Roman imperial laws. Over the next few years his commission, led by the jurist Tribonian, adds a digest of Roman legal writings and a textbook for students, the whole later called the Corpus Juris Civilis.
significance: Rediscovered in Italy in the 11th century, it became the foundation of the civil law systems used across much of continental Europe, Latin America and beyond.

title: Hagia Sophia completed
summary: After a riot destroys the previous church, Emperor Justinian has the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus build a new Hagia Sophia ('Holy Wisdom') in Constantinople in under six years. Its enormous dome seems to float above a ring of windows.
significance: For centuries it was the largest church in the Christian world; after 1453 it became a mosque whose design inspired Ottoman architects, and it remains a landmark of world architecture.

title: Plague of Justinian
summary: Bubonic plague appears at Pelusium in Egypt in 541 and reaches Constantinople the next year, where contemporaries report thousands of deaths a day. DNA from victims' remains confirms it was caused by the same bacterium as the later Black Death. The plague keeps returning for some two centuries, and how many people it killed is still debated.
significance: It is the first well-documented outbreak of bubonic plague, and it may have weakened the Byzantine Empire just as Justinian tried to win back the West.

title: Buddhism reaches Japan
summary: According to the Nihon Shoki, an early Japanese chronicle, King Seong of the Korean kingdom of Baekje sends a Buddhist statue and scriptures to the Japanese court. Other sources give the date as 538. The new religion is opposed by some powerful clans but supported by the Soga clan, and later by Prince Shotoku.
significance: Buddhism became, alongside Shinto, one of Japan's two main religious traditions, bringing temples such as Horyu-ji, art and learning from the Asian mainland.

title: Gokturk Khaganate founded
summary: Bumin, a leader of the Turks, who serve the Rouran nomad empire as ironworkers, revolts, defeats his overlords and takes the title of khagan. Within a few decades his successors rule a vast steppe empire stretching from Mongolia toward the Black Sea.
significance: It was the first state to bear the name 'Turk', and its later Orkhon inscriptions are the oldest known texts in a Turkic language, a heritage claimed by Turkic peoples from Turkey to Central Asia.

title: Tiwanaku and Wari states

location.name: Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca (one of the two centers)

summary: In the Andes, two powerful states rise. Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca in today's Bolivia, builds monumental stone temples and gateways and feeds its people with raised farm fields, while Wari, centered near Ayacucho in Peru, builds administrative centers and roads across much of the Peruvian highlands. How far either should be called an empire is debated.
significance: They were the first large states of the Andean highlands, and their roads, centers and ways of organizing labor foreshadowed the later Inca Empire.

title: Sui dynasty builds the Grand Canal

location.name: Luoyang (hub of the Sui canal network)

summary: Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty orders millions of laborers to dig and link canals joining the Yellow River and the Yangtze, connecting the rich farmlands of the south with the political centers of the north. Parts of the system already existed, and most of the work is finished within a few years.
significance: Expanded by later dynasties, the Grand Canal became the longest artificial waterway in the world and a lifeline of China's economy, though its huge cost in forced labor helped bring down the Sui in 618.

title: Harsha's empire in North India
summary: Harsha becomes king of Thanesar at the age of about 16 and soon also rules Kannauj, which he makes his capital. Through wars and alliances he dominates much of northern India, though his advance south is stopped by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II.
significance: Harsha's reign, described by his court poet Bana and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, was the last time for centuries that one ruler from northern India held such a large realm before the region split into rival kingdoms.

title: Muhammad's first revelation
summary: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca aged about 40, is meditating in a cave on Mount Hira when the angel Gabriel appears and commands him to 'Recite!'. These words begin the revelations that Muslims believe continue for the rest of his life and are collected in the Quran.
significance: It marks the beginning of Islam, which grew into one of the world's largest religions, with nearly two billion followers today.

title: Tang dynasty founded
summary: Li Yuan, a general of the collapsing Sui dynasty, seizes power and founds the Tang with its capital at Chang'an. The city grows into one of the largest and most cosmopolitan in the world, at the eastern end of the Silk Road.
significance: The Tang is remembered as a golden age of Chinese poetry, art and trade, and its culture and institutions shaped Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

title: The Hijra to Medina
summary: Facing growing hostility in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers move north to the oasis town of Yathrib, later called Medina, where he becomes the town's leader and organizes the first Muslim community.
significance: The Islamic calendar counts its years from the Hijra, which marks the start of Islam as a political as well as religious community.

title: Early Islamic conquests
summary: After Muhammad's death, the first caliphs unite Arabia and send armies against the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, both worn out by decades of war with each other. Within about thirty years the Arabs take Syria, Iraq, Egypt and most of Iran, bringing the Sasanian Empire to an end. Most people in the conquered lands convert to Islam only gradually, over the following centuries.
significance: The conquests created a new empire stretching from North Africa to Iran, in which Arabic and Islam spread and lasting borders between the Muslim and Christian worlds took shape.

title: Taika reforms in Japan
summary: Prince Naka no Oe and Nakatomi no Kamatari overthrow the powerful Soga clan in a palace coup and launch reforms to build a centralized state on the Chinese Tang model, with land owned by the throne, a census and taxes collected by officials. How much of the reform edict recorded in the Nihon Shoki dates from this time is debated.
significance: The reforms helped turn the Yamato kingdom into a centralized imperial state ruled by law codes, and Kamatari's descendants, the Fujiwara clan, dominated the Japanese court for centuries.

title: Srivijaya maritime empire rises
summary: From its base at Palembang on Sumatra, the Buddhist kingdom of Srivijaya extends its power over the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, the sea lanes linking India and China. Inscriptions from the 680s record its kings' expeditions, and the Chinese monk Yijing stays there to study Sanskrit.
significance: For centuries Srivijaya dominated trade through maritime Southeast Asia and was a major center of Buddhist learning.

title: Umayyad Caliphate founded
summary: After the murder of the caliph Ali, Muawiya, governor of Syria and a member of the Umayyad clan of Mecca, becomes caliph and rules from Damascus. He turns the caliphate into a hereditary dynasty.
significance: Under his successors the Umayyads expanded the caliphate from Spain to Central Asia and built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, while the struggles over the succession deepened the split between what became Sunni and Shia Islam.

title: Kanem Empire

location.name: Kanem, northeast of Lake Chad (capital Njimi, location uncertain)

summary: Northeast of Lake Chad, nomadic peoples found the kingdom of Kanem, which grows by controlling trade routes across the Sahara to the Fezzan in today's Libya. Its early history is known mostly from later chronicles and Arab writers, and its founding date is uncertain.
significance: Kanem and its successor Bornu lasted, under one dynasty or another, for about a thousand years, making it one of Africa's longest-lived states; its rulers adopted Islam in the 11th century.

title: Umayyad conquest of Iberia
summary: Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber commander serving the Umayyad caliphate, crosses from North Africa at Gibraltar, which is named after him (Jabal Tariq, 'Tariq's mountain'). He defeats the Visigothic king Roderic, and within a few years Muslim forces control most of the Iberian Peninsula.
significance: Muslim-ruled al-Andalus, centered on Cordoba, became a meeting place of Islamic, Jewish and Christian culture, until the Christian kingdoms of the north completed their reconquest in 1492.

title: Arab conquest of Sindh
summary: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, a young Umayyad general, captures the port of Debal near the mouth of the Indus, defeats King Dahir of Sindh and takes control of Sindh and southern Punjab, in today's Pakistan.
significance: Sindh became the first lasting foothold of Muslim rule in South Asia, linking the Indus region to the trade and scholarship of the Islamic world.

title: Battle of Tours

location.name: Between Tours and Poitiers (exact site uncertain)

summary: Frankish forces under Charles Martel defeat an Umayyad army from al-Andalus led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who is killed in the battle, somewhere between Poitiers and Tours in western France. Some historians date the battle to 733.
significance: Later writers often hailed it as saving Christian Europe from Islamic conquest, a view many historians now consider exaggerated, but it strengthened Charles Martel's family, the Carolingians.

title: Abbasid Caliphate founded

location.name: Kufa (where the first Abbasid caliph was proclaimed)

summary: A revolt that began in Khorasan, in eastern Iran, defeats the last Umayyad caliph at the Battle of the Zab in northern Iraq. Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah, a descendant of Muhammad's uncle Abbas, already proclaimed caliph at Kufa, founds the Abbasid dynasty. Many members of the Umayyad family are massacred, though one, Abd al-Rahman, escapes to Spain.
significance: The Abbasids moved the center of the Islamic world east to Iraq, and under later caliphs their capital Baghdad became the heart of a golden age of trade, science and scholarship.

title: Battle of Talas

location.name: Talas River, near Taraz (exact site uncertain)

summary: An Abbasid army defeats Tang Chinese forces near the Talas River, in today's Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, reportedly after the Tang army's Karluk Turk allies change sides. A famous story says Chinese prisoners taken here taught papermaking in Samarkand, but historians think paper had probably reached Central Asia earlier.
significance: It marked the westernmost reach of Tang China, which soon lost its hold on Central Asia during the An Lushan Rebellion, leaving the region open to Islamic and Turkic influence.

title: An Lushan Rebellion

location.name: Fanyang, near present-day Beijing (An Lushan's base)

summary: An Lushan, a powerful Tang general of Sogdian and Turkic descent, rebels from his base in the northeast and captures both Tang capitals, Luoyang and Chang'an. The war lasts until 763. Census figures fall dramatically, but historians think this partly reflects the collapse of record-keeping as well as mass deaths.
significance: The Tang survived, but much weakened: regional governors gained lasting power, and China lost control of Central Asia.

title: Baghdad founded
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds a new capital on the Tigris River, close to where it nears the Euphrates, built as a great round city with the caliph's palace and mosque at its center. Its location on river and caravan routes draws merchants from across Asia.
significance: Baghdad grew into one of the largest and richest cities in the world and a center of scholarship where Greek, Persian and Indian learning was translated into Arabic.

title: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
summary: Raiders from Scandinavia attack the monastery on the island of Lindisfarne, off the coast of Northumbria in northeastern England, killing monks and carrying off treasures and captives. The scholar Alcuin writes that such terror had never before appeared in Britain.
significance: The raid is traditionally seen as the start of the Viking Age, when Norse raiders, traders and settlers reached from North America to the Caspian Sea.

title: Borobudur built
summary: In central Java, rulers of the Sailendra dynasty build Borobudur, a vast Buddhist monument shaped as a stepped mountain topped by stupas. Pilgrims walking up its terraces pass more than 2,600 carved relief panels and over 500 statues of the Buddha. Construction probably takes several decades.
significance: Often described as the largest Buddhist monument in the world, Borobudur shows how deeply Indian religion and art had taken root in island Southeast Asia.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: On Christmas Day, Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne, king of the Franks and Lombards, as emperor in Rome. Charlemagne already rules much of western and central Europe, from the Pyrenees to the Elbe.
significance: It revived the title of emperor in the West for the first time since 476 and tied together the papacy, the Frankish monarchy and the Roman imperial idea, laying foundations for medieval Europe and the later Holy Roman Empire.

title: Khmer Empire founded
summary: According to an inscription written some 250 years later, Jayavarman II proclaims himself universal monarch in a ceremony on Phnom Kulen, a mountain in today's Cambodia, declaring independence from 'Java'. He unites rival Khmer principalities into one kingdom.
significance: The Khmer Empire, ruling from Angkor, dominated much of mainland Southeast Asia for centuries, and its later kings built Angkor Wat, often described as the largest religious monument in the world.

title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
summary: In Baghdad, the Persian scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi writes a book on solving equations by 'completion and balancing', in Arabic al-jabr. He also writes on the Indian system of numerals, including zero.
significance: The word 'algebra' comes from his book's title and 'algorithm' from his name, and Latin translations of his works helped bring algebra and Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe.

title: Chaco Canyon great houses
summary: In a dry canyon in what is now New Mexico, Ancestral Puebloan people begin building 'great houses', huge multi-story stone buildings such as Pueblo Bonito, with hundreds of rooms and round ceremonial chambers called kivas. Chaco grows into a center linked by straight roads to settlements across the region.
significance: Chaco was the largest center of the ancient American Southwest until its decline in the 1100s, and modern Pueblo peoples regard it as an ancestral place.

title: Gunpowder discovered
summary: Chinese Taoist alchemists, possibly searching for an elixir of immortality, find that mixing saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal makes a mixture that burns fiercely. A text often dated to the mid-9th century warns that such mixtures can burn the hands and face, but the date of the discovery is uncertain.
significance: By the 10th century gunpowder was used in Chinese warfare; it later spread across Asia and to Europe, where guns and cannons transformed war and the power of states.

title: Diamond Sutra, oldest dated printed book

location.name: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang (where it was found)

summary: A Chinese copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture, is printed from carved wooden blocks onto a paper scroll about 5 meters long. A note at its end says a man named Wang Jie had it made for his parents in the year corresponding to 868. Sealed in a cave at Dunhuang, it was found in 1900.
significance: It is the oldest known printed book with a date, showing that woodblock printing was already a mature craft in Tang China.

title: Kievan Rus founded
summary: According to the Primary Chronicle, written over two centuries later, Oleg, a leader of the Varangians (Scandinavian traders and warriors), seizes Kiev on the Dnieper River and makes it the center of a realm stretching north to Novgorod. The account is partly legendary.
significance: Kievan Rus became a large state on the trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium, adopted Orthodox Christianity in 988, and is claimed as a common ancestor by Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

title: Classic Maya collapse
summary: Over the 8th and 9th centuries, the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands, such as Tikal, Copan and Palenque, stop raising dated monuments, their kings disappear and most of their people move away. Its causes are debated; leading explanations include severe droughts, endless warfare and overuse of the land.
significance: Maya civilization did not end: cities in the northern Yucatan such as Chichen Itza flourished afterward, and millions of Maya people live in the region today.

title: Polynesians settle Hawaii
summary: Polynesian voyagers, probably from the Marquesas or Society Islands, sail thousands of kilometers across open ocean in double-hulled canoes and settle the Hawaiian Islands, bringing crops such as taro and animals such as pigs. The date is debated: older estimates were earlier, and recent radiocarbon studies suggest around 1000 to 1200.
significance: The settlement of Hawaii was one of the great feats of navigation without instruments, part of the Polynesian expansion that reached nearly every habitable island of the Pacific.

title: Fatimid Caliphate founded
summary: Kutama Berber forces, won over by an Ismaili Shia missionary, overthrow the Aghlabid rulers of Ifriqiya (today's Tunisia). Their leader Abdallah al-Mahdi, who claims descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, is proclaimed caliph early in 910, challenging the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad.
significance: The Fatimids later conquered Egypt and founded Cairo, and for two centuries their rival Shia caliphate was a major power in the Mediterranean world.

title: Song dynasty founded
summary: Zhao Kuangyin, a general of the Later Zhou, is proclaimed emperor by his troops and founds the Song dynasty with its capital at Kaifeng. Over the following two decades the Song reunite most of China after half a century of division.
significance: Song China saw a commercial boom, the first government-issued paper money, wider use of printing and the compass, and a civil service chosen by examinations.

title: Holy Roman Empire founded
summary: Otto I, king of Germany, who had defeated the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955, is crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII. Some historians instead date the empire's beginning to Charlemagne's coronation in 800, and the name 'Holy Roman Empire' only came into use later.
significance: The empire, a loose union of German, Italian and other lands under an elected emperor, lasted until 1806 and shaped the politics and borders of central Europe.

title: Rajaraja Chola expands the Chola Empire
summary: Rajaraja I becomes king of the Cholas of Tamil Nadu and conquers neighboring kingdoms in southern India, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives, using a strong navy. At his capital Thanjavur he builds the Brihadisvara Temple, completed around 1010.
significance: Under Rajaraja and his son Rajendra I, the Chola Empire became the leading power of southern India and the Bay of Bengal, spreading Tamil culture and trade across the sea to Southeast Asia.

title: Norse reach Vinland
summary: Norse sailors from the settlements in Greenland, led according to Icelandic sagas by Leif Erikson, reach a land they call Vinland on the coast of North America. Remains of their camp at L'Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland, include wood cut with metal tools, which a tree-ring study dates to 1021. They do not stay long.
significance: It was the first known European contact with the Americas, nearly five centuries before Columbus, though it left no lasting settlement.
